newsitem.title: CHINA: Hong Kong housing heads agenda, supply to rise.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong housing heads agenda, supply to rise.

text.p: Hong Kong's fledgling government has released forecasts suggesting a dramatic increase in the supply of flats in the overcrowded territory.

The statements, released on Wednesday, appeared to confirm earlier promises that the housing issue tops the agenda of the new government of this special region of China, created on July 1 after 156 years of British rule.

Following Tuesday's announcement of a substantial increase in land supply, Financial Secretary Donald Tsang said he was confident of attaining a target of at least 85,000 new flats a year for the next eight years.
"My colleagues and I have the confidence that we can reach the (target) given to us by the chief executive (Tung Chee-hwa)," Tsang told reporters.
"And for the long term, our task to resolve the housing problem, we do have confidence we can resolve it."

At least 79,000 new flats would be released into Hong Kong's thirsty property market each year for the next three years, he said. Thereafter, about 104,000 new flats would be released each year until 2004/05.

The forecasts were a substantial increase over estimated 1997 production of 60,000 flats, and followed Tuesday's announcement of a whopping 140 percent increase in land supply over the next five years.

The new government's obvious determination to tackle Hong Kong's property crisis could compromise real estate prices in the short-term, but most analysts said earlier they were still expecting a rise of about 10 percent both this year and next.
Tsang on Wednesday said the government was more concerned with providing a steady, sufficient supply of housing than influencing Hong Kong's overheated property market.
But he conceded that some property price erosion was inevitable as these new measures took hold.

"We don't have any expectation on property prices. We just want to have a stable supply of flats," he said. "Hong Kong's market is very efficient. I think there will be (some) adjustment. But of course the ultimate result is that property prices will be eased as a result of sufficient supply."

The difficulty of obtaining reasonably-priced housing ranks as the number one concern for ordinary people in Hong Kong, and has grabbed most of the new government's attention during its first few days in power.
A property cartel has long been accused of keeping prices artificially high. Sky-high rents are now accused of undermining Hong Kong's competitiveness.
Tung issued a broad policy outline on his plan to confront the problem hours after being sworn in as Chief Executive on July 1, replacing the last colonial governor, Chris Patten.
Tung's ambitious agenda includes home ownership rates of 70 percent within 10 years -- a substantial increase over current levels of about 50 percent.
He also wants land reclamation to be sped up, public housing to be sold and the waiting list for public rental housing to be cut to three years.
Further details of the government's plans to meet these goals will be outlined in a policy speech by Tung in October.
Tsang also said he would release more information, including the economic impact of these proposals, in his 1998/99 budget next March.
